name: Aerospike
license: AGPL-3.0 (Community Edition server), Apache 2.0 (clients); Enterprise Edition proprietary
summary: A distributed key-value database written in C that keeps its index in RAM and its records on SSDs, for steady sub-millisecond lookups on terabytes of data.
intro: Aerospike stores records under keys, grouped into namespaces (like databases) and sets (like tables); a record holds named bins, like columns, whose types come from their values. Each namespace picks its own storage: records can live in RAM or, more cheaply, on SSDs, where Aerospike writes to the flash device directly and bypasses the file system. The primary index stays in RAM by default and costs 64 bytes per record whatever the record’s size, so a lookup is one hash and one device read. Records can expire with a time to live.

A key is hashed with RIPEMD-160, and 12 bits of the digest pick one of 4,096 partitions per namespace, spread evenly over the nodes. Each partition has one master copy and replicas on other nodes, two copies in total being the common setting, and the cluster rebalances partitions by itself when nodes join or leave. Clients learn the partition map and send each request straight to the node that owns the key, with no proxy in between. Cross-datacenter replication (XDR) ships changes to clusters elsewhere.

A namespace runs in one of two modes. Availability mode, the default, keeps serving during network splits but can lose writes or return stale data. Strong consistency mode, available in the Enterprise Edition and the managed cloud, never loses an acknowledged write and offers linearizable reads. Aerospike 8.0, released in January 2025, added transactions across records in one namespace with strict serializability; 8.2, from September 2026, is the current release. The Community Edition server is AGPL-3.0, while strong consistency, index-on-flash and other features are in the paid Enterprise Edition.
strengths: Predictable latency at large data sizes: index in RAM, data on SSD, one device read per lookup
Smart clients go straight to the node that owns a key, and partitions rebalance on their own
Choose per namespace between availability and strong consistency, with multi-record transactions since 8.0
Much cheaper per terabyte than keeping everything in memory, as Redis or Memcached do
limits: Every record costs 64 bytes of RAM in the index on every node that holds a copy, so billions of tiny records need a lot of memory
Strong consistency, index-on-flash and other operational features are only in the paid Enterprise Edition
In the default availability mode, a network split can lose acknowledged writes or serve stale reads

goodFor.why: The primary index stays in RAM and clients send each request straight to the node that owns the key, so a lookup is one hash and one device read.
Since 8.0, transactions can span records anywhere in one namespace and are strictly serializable.

specs.data-model: Records of named bins under keys, grouped in namespaces and sets
specs.query-language: Key-value operations through smart client libraries
specs.transactions: Multi-record within one namespace, strictly serializable (since 8.0)
specs.consistency: Per namespace: availability mode (default) or strong consistency (Enterprise)
specs.scaling: 4,096 hash partitions per namespace, rebalanced automatically
specs.replication: One master and replicas per partition; two copies is common
specs.storage-engine: Primary index in RAM (64 bytes per record); data in RAM or on raw SSD
specs.deployment: Self-hosted Community (AGPL) or Enterprise Edition, or Aerospike’s managed cloud

story: Aerospike started as Citrusleaf, a key-value database sold from 2010. In August 2012 the company and product were renamed Aerospike, and the same year it bought AlchemyDB and folded in its features. Its design kept indexes in memory and let the records themselves live on flash, written without a file system in between.

In 2014 Aerospike open-sourced the server under the AGPL and its client libraries under Apache 2.0, while keeping an Enterprise Edition. Version 4.0 in 2018 added a strong consistency mode beside the default available one, and 6.x added JSON documents and queries. Aerospike 8.0 in January 2025 brought distributed ACID transactions across records, and it now also offers graph and vector search models alongside key-value and documents.

choices.choice: Index in RAM, records on SSD
choices.why: SSDs hold far more data per dollar than RAM. Keeping only the fixed-size index in memory means finding a record never touches disk, and reading it takes one device read.

choices.choice: Write to raw flash, not files
choices.why: Bypassing the file system gives Aerospike control over how data is laid out and written on SSDs, and removes a layer of caching and overhead.

choices.choice: A fixed set of partitions and smart clients
choices.why: With 4,096 partitions per namespace and the map held by clients, every request goes to the right node in one hop and rebalancing moves whole partitions.

Version 4.0 adds a strong consistency mode
